title: Controlling the Coupling Strengths in Nanophotonic Networks using Modified Yagi-Uda Nanoplasmonic Antennas
abstract: On-chip communication in optical neural networks is commonly done via waveguides which results in large system footprints. A compact alternative is to broadcast light signals between nano-optoelectronic components in free space and tailor the light field distribution using sub-wavelength nanophotonics. We propose and simulate nanoplasmonic metal structures in combination with III-V nanowire emitters and receivers to create an optical network in which the shape and position of these nanostructures create varying weights between the nano-optoelectronic nodes. Using Finite Difference Time Domain modelling, we investigate systems of experimentally verified nanowire optoelectronics combined with nanoplasmonic structures that can be made in the same fabrication step as electrical contacts powering the nanowires. We investigate both individual nanowire/antenna devices as well as networks corresponding to two layers in a neural network. We show that directed communication from a nanowire node can be significantly altered using Yagi-Uda antennas. Modifying the antenna with an asymmetric director component enables the directing of light several different angular directions simultaneously. We find that highly variable complex weight distribution between the connections in two seven node layers can be achieved depending on the combined geometry of the antenna components. The possible weight distributions in compact layers of nanowire nodes could be used for creating a variety of neural networks with complex connectivity. The concepts can be generalized to other types of nanoscale emitter/receiver systems.
summary: This paper proposes using modified Yagi-Uda nanoplasmonic antennas integrated with III-V nanowires to create compact optical interconnects for neural networks. By precisely controlling the antenna geometry, the authors demonstrate the ability to engineer highly variable coupling strengths, enabling the realization of complex artificial synaptic weight matrices on a chip.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for compact alternatives to traditional waveguides for implementing optical neural networks on a chip.
main_result: By using modified Yagi-Uda nanoplasmonic antennas, the authors demonstrated the ability to achieve highly variable and complex weight distributions between connected nodes in artificial neural network layers.
method: The study relies on simulating the interaction of light with nanoplasmonic structures using Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) methods.
model_or_system: The physical system combines III-V nanowire emitters/receivers with nanoplasmonic metal structures, specifically modified Yagi-Uda antennas. This setup is designed to mimic the connectivity and weight calculation of artificial neural network layers.
key_observables: Power absorption ($	ext{Pabs}$) on the receiver, forward/backward scattering cross-section, and the complex weight distribution between nodes.
important_parameters: Nanowire dimensions ($L=3 \mu	ext{m}, r=88 	ext{ nm}$), antenna director dimensions (e.g., $[D_x, D_y, D_z] = [485, 350, 60]$ nm), and director separation (750 nm).
main_assumptions: The underlying substrate is $	ext{SiO}_2$ on $	ext{Si}$, and the nanowires are assumed to function as building blocks capable of non-linear evaluation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the basic concept, showing symmetric and modified Yagi-Uda designs, and detail the forward/backward scattering cross-section and power absorption fraction as a function of antenna director parameters.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of compact on-chip optical communication, proposes the nanoplasmonic/Yagi-Uda antenna solution, details the simulation methodology (FDTD), presents results showing directional control and weight tunability, and concludes by discussing the potential for complex network realization.
why_interesting: While the core physics is classical electromagnetism, the application directly models artificial synapses and network connectivity, linking advanced photonics to computational models relevant to neuromorphic computing research.
